---
title: "Projections — The Shadow of an Arrow"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

A flashlight casts a vector's shadow onto a horizontal line. How long is that shadow?

## Build the intuition

Orthogonal projection extracts the component of one vector along a chosen nonzero direction.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}(\mathbf v)=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\mathbf u
$$

**Every symbol explained:** proj means projection; v is the vector we want to project; u is the nonzero direction; the dot means dot product; the fraction gives the scalar amount of u needed to reach the nearest point on the line through u.

**Substitute real numbers:** Take v=(3,4), u=(1,0). Dot products are v·u=3 and u·u=1; projection=(3/1)(1,0)=(3,0). The perpendicular leftover is (0,4).

## Why the relationship is true

The error v−projection is perpendicular to u: (0,4)·(1,0)=0. That orthogonality is why the projection is the closest point on the line.

## Where the shortcut stops working

The formula divides by u·u, so u must not be the zero vector. An oblique projection is a different operation.

## Your turn

Project (3,4) onto u=(0,2). Why does the answer not depend on how long u is?

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Geometric aspects, §§4.2–4.3. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
